description: Description and security rationale for every Audit.ps1 check. Audit.ps1 prints them under every failed check and reads no other file for them. checks lists the checks whose name does not start with a CIS number; checks named 'CIS <id> ...' take their text from cisRecommendations by that number.
notes: checks is written by hand. name is the check name exactly as Audit.ps1 prints it.
cisIds: the check covers these CIS recommendations, so the description and rationale come from cisRecommendations in this file.

Otherwise description and rationale summarize the listed sources (Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Support, MITRE ATT&CK, IETF RFCs, Chrome Enterprise). An empty rationale means no trustworthy source stating the security reason was found.
verifiedOn is the date the sources of checks were read.

cisBenchmark and cisRecommendations are generated by Update-AuditCheckDetails.ps1: a copy of id, title, printed page, description and rationale from CIS_Microsoft_Windows_11_Stand-alone_Benchmark_v5.0.0.json for every recommendation Audit.ps1 checks. Do not edit them by hand, and keep them as the last two properties; run the script again instead.

checks.name: Secure Boot
checks.description: Secure Boot is a UEFI firmware standard that helps make sure the PC boots only software trusted by the device manufacturer. When the PC starts, the firmware checks the signature of each piece of boot software, including UEFI firmware drivers, EFI applications and the operating system, and boots only if the signatures are valid.
checks.rationale: Only signed, trusted boot components can run before Windows and its antimalware software start, so malware cannot replace the boot loader or load untrusted code early in the boot process. The revoked-signatures database (dbx) also stops boot components that are known to be bad from loading.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Secure boot

checks.name: TPM 2.0 Status
checks.description: The Trusted Platform Module (TPM) is a tamper-resistant secure crypto-processor. It generates, stores and limits the use of cryptographic keys, and it records security measurements of the boot process.
checks.rationale: Keys held in the TPM can be made unusable outside it, so they cannot be copied and used elsewhere, and its dictionary-attack logic stops repeated guessing of a key's authorization value. The boot measurements make sure a TPM-based key is used only when the correct software booted the system; BitLocker and device health attestation depend on this.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Trusted Platform Module technology overview

checks.name: Built-in Administrator Account
checks.description: The built-in Administrator account (SID ending in -500) is the first account Windows creates. It has full control of the files, directories, services and other resources on the device. Windows setup disables it and creates another administrator account instead.
checks.rationale: The account is known to exist on every Windows installation, so Microsoft recommends disabling it to make it more difficult for malicious users to gain access. Renaming it is not enough, because a renamed Administrator account keeps the same well-known SID.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Local accounts (Administrator, security considerations)

checks.name: Cached Logon Credentials
checks.description: Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache. Sets how many unique users' domain sign-in information Windows caches locally, so a user can still sign in when a domain controller can't be contacted. The default is 10.
checks.rationale: An attacker who can access the file system could locate the cached sign-in information and use a brute-force attack to try to determine user passwords. Microsoft's countermeasure is 0 (no caching); 2 is suggested for end-user computers that must sign in away from the domain.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache

checks.name: Defender Real-Time Protection
checks.description: Real-time protection in Microsoft Defender Antivirus scans files and activity as they are opened, downloaded or run, together with behavior monitoring and heuristics.
checks.rationale: Microsoft warns that disabling real-time protection drastically reduces the protection on the device, because malware is then found only by a scheduled scan, after it has already run.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Configure Microsoft Defender Antivirus always-on protection

checks.name: Defender Cloud-Delivered Protection (MAPS)
checks.description: Cloud-delivered protection (Microsoft Advanced Protection Service, MAPS) lets Defender ask Microsoft's cloud services and machine learning about files it does not recognize. Basic reports less information than Advanced; both count as turned on.
checks.rationale: Cloud protection identifies new threats far faster than regular security intelligence updates, sometimes before a single device is infected, and Microsoft recommends keeping it turned on.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Cloud protection and Microsoft Defender Antivirus

checks.name: Defender Sample Submission
checks.description: Sample submission controls whether Defender sends suspicious files to Microsoft for analysis: always prompt (0), send safe samples automatically (1), never send (2) or send all samples (3). This check only requires that it is not set to never send; it does not require sending all samples.
checks.rationale: Without samples, Microsoft cannot analyze a new threat that cloud protection flags as suspicious, so the protection for unknown files is weaker. Sending samples is a privacy choice, which is why safe samples and being prompted are accepted.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Cloud protection and Microsoft Defender Antivirus

checks.name: Defender Cloud Protection Level
checks.description: The cloud block level sets how aggressively Defender blocks files that the cloud service has no clear verdict for: default (0), moderate (1), high (2), high plus (4) or zero tolerance (6). The Microsoft security baseline for Windows 11 26H2 uses High.
checks.rationale: A higher level blocks more unknown and suspicious files before they run, which stops new malware that is not yet known. The cost is that a few legitimate but rare files, such as self-built programs, can be blocked until they are allowed.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Specify the cloud protection level
Microsoft Security Compliance Toolkit: security baseline for Windows 11 26H2 (Select cloud protection level)

checks.name: Defender Extended Cloud Check
checks.description: The extended cloud check lets Defender hold a suspicious file for up to 50 more seconds while it waits for the cloud verdict before the file runs. The Microsoft security baseline for Windows 11 26H2 sets it to the maximum, 50 seconds.
checks.rationale: Giving the cloud service more time to analyze an unknown file means fewer new threats run before a verdict arrives. The cost is a delay of up to 50 seconds the first time an unknown file is opened.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Cloud protection and Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Microsoft Security Compliance Toolkit: security baseline for Windows 11 26H2 (Configure extended cloud check)

checks.name: Defender Removable Drive Scanning
checks.description: When removable drive scanning is on, Defender's full scans also scan USB sticks and other removable drives that are connected during the scan. It is on in the Microsoft security baseline for Windows 11 26H2; Windows turns it off by default.
checks.rationale: USB drives are a common way for malware to reach a PC. Scanning them in full scans finds malware that is stored on a drive that is plugged in, before it spreads. The cost is a longer full scan when a large drive is connected.

checks.name: Defender Tamper Protection
checks.description: Tamper protection keeps important Microsoft Defender security settings from being disabled or changed. While it is on, real-time protection, behavior monitoring, cloud protection and security intelligence updates stay enabled, exclusions can't be added, and changes to Defender settings through the registry are blocked.
checks.rationale: During cyberattacks, attackers often try to disable security features on devices to access data, install malware, and exploit data, identities and devices. Tamper protection stops these changes.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Tamper protection overview

checks.name: Defender Antivirus Service
checks.description: The Microsoft Defender Antivirus service (WinDefend, MsMpEng.exe) is the antivirus and anti-malware engine built into Windows. In active mode it scans files, remediates threats and lists detected threats in the Windows Security app.
checks.rationale: When Microsoft Defender Antivirus is disabled or uninstalled, files aren't scanned and threats aren't remediated. Microsoft does not recommend disabling it.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Microsoft Defender Antivirus in Windows overview

checks.name: Defender Signature Age
checks.description: Microsoft Defender Antivirus uses security intelligence (signature) updates to recognize threats. The check fails when the installed security intelligence is older than the allowed number of days.
checks.rationale: Microsoft says it is important to keep the antivirus up to date: regular updates make sure the device has the latest technology to protect against new malware and attack techniques. Outdated security intelligence misses recent threats.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Microsoft Defender Antivirus in Windows overview (antivirus updates)
Microsoft Learn: Manage Microsoft Defender Antivirus updates and apply baselines

checks.name: Windows Exploit Protection
checks.description: Exploit protection applies exploit mitigation techniques to the operating system and apps. The system-wide mitigations checked here are Data Execution Prevention (DEP, stops code from running in data-only memory pages), Control Flow Guard (CFG, checks the targets of indirect calls), Bottom-up ASLR (randomizes the locations of memory allocations) and SEHOP (checks the integrity of the exception chain).
checks.rationale: Exploit protection helps protect devices from malware that uses exploits to infect them and spread. These mitigations make memory-corruption vulnerabilities much harder to exploit.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Exploit protection reference

checks.name: Potentially Unwanted App (PUA) Protection
checks.description: Potentially unwanted applications (PUA) are software that can make the PC run slowly, display unexpected ads, or install other unexpected or unwanted software. PUA protection lets Microsoft Defender Antivirus detect and block them.
checks.rationale: Microsoft notes that PUA can increase the risk of the network being infected with actual malware, make malware infections harder to identify, and waste resources on cleaning up the applications.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Detect and block potentially unwanted applications

checks.name: Defender Network Protection
checks.description: Network protection is an attack surface reduction capability of Microsoft Defender that blocks connections from applications to dangerous domains, such as domains that host phishing scams, exploits and other malicious content. It extends Microsoft Defender SmartScreen to outbound traffic from all applications, not only the browser.
checks.rationale: It helps prevent users and applications from reaching dangerous domains that host phishing scams, exploits and other malicious content on the internet, also for programs that do not use SmartScreen themselves.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Turn on network protection

checks.name: Defender Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) Rules
checks.description: Attack surface reduction rules block specific software behaviors, such as Office apps creating child processes or executable content, scripts that download or run files, obfuscated scripts, and credential theft from LSASS.
checks.rationale: These behaviors occur in some legitimate software, but they are considered risky because attackers commonly abuse them through malware. Blocking them reduces the places where the PC can be attacked.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Attack surface reduction rules reference
Microsoft Learn: Attack surface reduction overview

checks.name: Controlled Folder Access (Ransomware)
checks.description: Controlled folder access allows only trusted apps to change files in protected folders, such as Documents, Pictures, Videos, Music and Desktop.
checks.rationale: It helps protect valuable data from malicious apps and threats such as ransomware, which encrypt or delete files in exactly these folders.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Protect important folders with controlled folder access

checks.name: Vulnerable Driver Blocklist
checks.description: The Microsoft vulnerable driver blocklist stops known-bad kernel drivers from loading. It is enforced when Memory Integrity (HVCI) or Smart App Control is on, and it is on by default for all devices starting with Windows 11 2022 Update.
checks.rationale: The blocklist covers non-Microsoft drivers with known security vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit to elevate privileges in the Windows kernel, drivers with malicious behavior or signed with certificates used to sign malware, and drivers that circumvent the Windows security model.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Microsoft recommended driver block rules

checks.name: SmartScreen for Microsoft Store Apps
checks.description: Microsoft Defender SmartScreen checks the web content that Microsoft Store apps use (EnableWebContentEvaluation).
checks.rationale: Microsoft Defender SmartScreen protects against phishing and malware websites and applications, and against downloading potentially malicious files; this setting extends that protection to web content loaded by Store apps.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Microsoft Defender SmartScreen overview

checks.name: Microsoft Defender SmartScreen (Edge)
checks.description: The SmartScreenEnabled policy turns on Microsoft Defender SmartScreen in Microsoft Edge and, because it is set by policy, users can't turn it off.
checks.rationale: SmartScreen in Edge helps protect users from phishing and malware websites and from downloading potentially malicious files, by checking sites and downloads against a list of reported malicious sites and files.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Microsoft Defender SmartScreen in Microsoft Edge

checks.name: Edge SmartScreen Potentially Unwanted App Blocking
checks.description: The SmartScreenPuaEnabled policy turns on blocking of potentially unwanted apps with Microsoft Defender SmartScreen in Microsoft Edge.
checks.rationale: Potentially unwanted app blocking shows warnings that help protect users from adware, coin miners, bundleware and other low-reputation apps hosted by websites.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Edge policy SmartScreenPuaEnabled

checks.name: Edge Password Export
checks.description: The PasswordExportEnabled policy controls whether the Export passwords button in the Microsoft Edge password manager (edge://wallet/passwords) is available. When it is disabled, saved passwords can't be exported.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Edge policy PasswordExportEnabled

checks.name: Edge Browsing Data Lifetime
checks.description: The BrowsingDataLifetime policy makes Microsoft Edge periodically delete the selected types of browsing data (here browsing history, download history and cached images and files) that are older than the set number of hours. The policy has no effect while Edge sync is on.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Edge policy BrowsingDataLifetime

checks.name: Chrome Browsing Data Lifetime
checks.description: The BrowsingDataLifetime policy makes Google Chrome automatically remove the selected types of browsing data (here browsing history, download history and cached images and files) that are older than the set number of hours. Starting with Chrome 115, the policy turns off sync for those data types.

sources.title: Chrome Enterprise: BrowsingDataLifetime policy

checks.name: Edge Extension Install Policy
checks.description: The ExtensionInstallBlocklist policy with the value * blocks all Microsoft Edge extensions by default; only signed extensions on the allow-list (ExtensionInstallAllowlist) can be installed. Blocked extensions that are already installed are disabled, and users can't turn them back on.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Edge policy ExtensionInstallBlocklist
Microsoft Learn: Edge policy ExtensionInstallAllowlist

checks.name: Chrome Extension Install Policy
checks.description: The ExtensionInstallBlocklist policy with the value * blocks all Google Chrome extensions by default; only extensions on the allow-list can be installed. Blocked extensions that are already installed are disabled, and users can't turn them back on.

sources.title: Chrome Enterprise: ExtensionInstallBlocklist policy

checks.name: Edge Installation Detection
checks.description: Determines whether Microsoft Edge is installed, so its browser policy checks run only when it is. This check fails only when the installation state cannot be determined.

checks.name: Chrome Installation Detection
checks.description: Determines whether Google Chrome is installed, so its browser policy checks run only when it is. This check fails only when the installation state cannot be determined.

checks.name: Public Network Profile Safety
checks.description: Windows assigns each network a profile. Public, the recommended default for new networks, hides the PC from other devices on the network and turns off file and printer sharing. Private makes the PC discoverable and allows sharing, and is meant only for networks whose people and devices you trust.
checks.rationale: On a network with the Public profile, other devices cannot discover the PC or reach its shared files and printers, which limits what an untrusted network, such as a hotel or café network, can see and attack.

sources.title: Microsoft Support: Essential network settings and tasks in Windows
Microsoft Learn: Windows Firewall overview

checks.name: Windows PowerShell 2.0
checks.description: Windows PowerShell 2.0 is a legacy PowerShell engine. It was deprecated in 2017 and is being removed from Windows, starting with Windows 11 version 24H2; PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7 remain available.
checks.rationale: Microsoft removes PowerShell 2.0 to improve Windows security, clean up legacy code and reduce the complexity of the PowerShell ecosystem.

sources.title: Microsoft Support: PowerShell 2.0 removal from Windows

checks.name: LLMNR Name Resolution
checks.description: Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR) is a Windows fallback method that resolves names on the local network by multicast when DNS cannot resolve them.
checks.rationale: Any device on the local network can answer an LLMNR request and pretend to be the requested host. The victim then sends its user name and NTLMv2 hash to the attacker, who can crack the hash offline or relay it to run code on another system. MITRE recommends disabling LLMNR when it is not needed.

sources.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1557.001: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay

checks.name: NetBIOS over TCP/IP
checks.description: NetBIOS over TCP/IP includes the NetBIOS Name Service (NBT-NS), a legacy broadcast method that maps computers to their NetBIOS names on the local network.
checks.rationale: Any device on the local network can answer an NBT-NS request and pretend to be the requested host. The victim then sends its user name and NTLMv2 hash to the attacker, who can crack the hash offline or relay it to run code on another system. MITRE recommends disabling NetBIOS when it is not needed.

sources.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1557.001: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay

checks.name: Windows Ready Print Driver Ranking
checks.description: Windows Ready Print driver ranking makes Windows prefer the Microsoft IPP Class Driver, which is built into Windows, for printers that support the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP), over a driver from the printer manufacturer. It applies when a printer is set up; printers that are already installed keep their driver.
checks.rationale: Printer drivers run inside the Print Spooler service, which runs as SYSTEM, and third-party print drivers have repeatedly been a way to attack it. The built-in class driver is maintained and updated by Microsoft through Windows Update, so preferring it reduces the amount of third-party code that runs with system rights. The Microsoft security baseline for Windows 11 26H2 enables this setting.

sources.title: Microsoft Security Compliance Toolkit: security baseline for Windows 11 26H2 (Configure Windows Ready Print driver ranking)

checks.name: Edge Internet Explorer Mode
checks.description: Internet Explorer mode lets Microsoft Edge open a page with the old Internet Explorer 11 engine. InternetExplorerIntegrationLevel = 0 (None) turns off IE mode for the whole browser, and InternetExplorerIntegrationReloadInIEModeAllowed = 0 stops users from reloading a site in IE mode themselves.
checks.rationale: Internet Explorer mode is the one way the retired Internet Explorer 11 engine can still run on Windows 11. That engine is old and has a long record of vulnerabilities, so a malicious page that makes Edge switch to it, or a user who is talked into reloading a page in IE mode, would be exposed to attacks that current Edge is protected against.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Edge policy InternetExplorerIntegrationLevel
Microsoft Learn: Edge policy InternetExplorerIntegrationReloadInIEModeAllowed

checks.name: Internet Explorer Launch via COM Automation
checks.description: The policy Disable Internet Explorer 11 Launch Via COM Automation stops programs from starting Internet Explorer 11 through COM automation (DisableInternetExplorerLaunchViaCOM = 1). iexplore.exe is still present on Windows 11, but only as a stub that opens Microsoft Edge.
checks.rationale: COM automation is a way for a program to start and drive Internet Explorer without any window the user would notice, and malware has used it to run the old engine. The Microsoft security baseline for Windows 11 26H2 enables this policy.

sources.title: Microsoft Security Compliance Toolkit: security baseline for Windows 11 26H2 (Disable Internet Explorer 11 Launch Via COM Automation)

checks.name: Lock Screen Widgets Disabled
checks.description: The lock screen widgets ("Weather and more") show small information cards, such as weather, on the Windows lock screen. The policy DisableWidgetsOnLockScreen under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Dsh turns them off for every user of the PC. The value 0 hides the widgets and 1 shows them (tested on Windows 11 build 10.0.26300), which matches the values table of the Microsoft documentation (0 = Enabled, 1 = Disabled) when its labels are read as the state of the policy. The behavior is as documented; only the name of the value is misleading, because it suggests the opposite. The check requires 0.
checks.rationale: The widgets fetch content from the internet and display it before anyone has signed in, which adds a network-fed component to the lock screen. Turning them off keeps the lock screen minimal. This is not a CIS or Microsoft baseline recommendation.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Policy CSP - NewsAndInterests

checks.name: Chrome Safe Browsing Protection Level
checks.description: The Chrome policy SafeBrowsingProtectionLevel sets Safe Browsing to standard (1) or enhanced (2) protection; 0 turns it off. Safe Browsing checks visited sites and downloads against Google's lists of phishing and malware sites.
checks.rationale: Safe Browsing is Chrome's main protection against phishing and malware sites, the most common way people are tricked into giving away passwords or installing malware. Setting the policy keeps it from being turned off.

sources.title: Google Chrome Enterprise policy documentation
CIS Google Chrome Group Policy Benchmark v1.1.1 (recommendation 2.15.2)

checks.name: Chrome Safe Browsing Warnings Cannot Be Bypassed
checks.description: The Chrome policy DisableSafeBrowsingProceedAnyway = 1 removes the option to continue to a page after a Safe Browsing warning.
checks.rationale: Phishing pages are built to make people click past warnings. Without the option to proceed, a warning stops the visit to a known malicious page.

sources.title: Google Chrome Enterprise policy documentation
CIS Google Chrome Group Policy Benchmark v1.1.1 (recommendation 2.15.3)

checks.name: Chrome Download Restrictions
checks.description: The Chrome policy DownloadRestrictions controls which downloads Chrome blocks. 4 blocks downloads that Safe Browsing identifies as malicious (Google's recommended value); 1, 2 and 3 block more (dangerous file types, potentially dangerous downloads, or all downloads).
checks.rationale: Without it, a user can keep a download that Safe Browsing has identified as malicious, and run it.

sources.title: Google Chrome Enterprise policy documentation
CIS Google Chrome Group Policy Benchmark v1.1.1 (recommendation 2.42)

checks.name: Chrome Component Updates
checks.description: The Chrome policy ComponentUpdatesEnabled = 1 keeps Chrome's components updating, such as the Safe Browsing lists and certificate revocation data, independently of Chrome itself.
checks.rationale: Outdated components weaken protections that depend on current data, for example Safe Browsing and certificate revocation checks.

sources.title: Google Chrome Enterprise policy documentation
CIS Google Chrome Group Policy Benchmark v1.1.1 (recommendation 2.37)

checks.name: Chrome Automatic Updates
checks.description: The Google Update policy "Update policy override" for Chrome (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Google\Update, value Update{8A69D345-D564-463C-AFF1-A69D9E530F96}): 0 = updates disabled, 1 = always allow updates, 2 = manual updates only, 3 = automatic updates only. 1 and 3 keep Chrome updating automatically.
checks.rationale: Browsers are attacked through known vulnerabilities, so security fixes must arrive quickly; an outdated Chrome is open to attacks that a current version blocks.

sources.title: Google Chrome Enterprise policy documentation
CIS Google Chrome Group Policy Benchmark v1.1.1 (recommendation 4.2)

checks.name: Chrome Remote Debugging Disabled
checks.description: The Chrome policy RemoteDebuggingAllowed = 0 stops Chrome from opening a remote debugging port, through which another program can control the browser.
checks.rationale: Information-stealing malware starts Chrome with remote debugging to read session cookies and take over signed-in accounts without needing the password.

sources.title: Google Chrome Enterprise policy documentation
CIS Google Chrome Group Policy Benchmark v1.1.1 (recommendation 2.69)

checks.name: Chrome Application-Bound Encryption
checks.description: The Chrome policy ApplicationBoundEncryptionEnabled = 1 keeps application-bound encryption on: Chrome encrypts cookies and saved passwords with a key bound to Chrome itself.
checks.rationale: Other programs running as the same user, such as information stealers, then cannot simply decrypt the cookies and passwords Chrome stores.

sources.title: Google Chrome Enterprise policy documentation
CIS Google Chrome Group Policy Benchmark v1.1.1 (recommendation 2.88)

checks.name: Teredo Tunneling
checks.description: Teredo is an IPv6 transition technology that tunnels IPv6 traffic inside IPv4 UDP packets, so a PC behind a NAT router can reach the IPv6 internet.
checks.rationale: Microsoft security bulletin MS07-038 notes that Teredo facilitates network tunneling, so communications could bypass network perimeter firewalls, and lists disabling Teredo as a workaround.

sources.title: Microsoft Security Bulletin MS07-038

checks.name: TLS/SSL Protocol Versions (Schannel)
checks.description: Schannel is the Windows component that implements SSL and TLS for Windows and many applications. The check requires SSL 2.0, SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 to be disabled and TLS 1.2 (and TLS 1.3 on Windows 11) to be enabled.
checks.rationale: The IETF has deprecated TLS 1.0 and 1.1 (RFC 8996) because they lack support for current and recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms, and has prohibited SSL 2.0 (RFC 6176) and deprecated SSL 3.0 (RFC 7568) because of known weaknesses such as the POODLE attack. Allowing them lets an attacker force or exploit a weak connection.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: TLS registry settings
Microsoft Learn: Solving the TLS 1.0 problem
IETF RFC 8996: Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1
IETF RFC 7568: Deprecating Secure Sockets Layer Version 3.0

checks.name: DNS over HTTPS (DoH)
checks.description: With DNS over HTTPS, DNS queries between the Windows DNS client and the DNS server pass through an encrypted HTTPS connection instead of plain text.
checks.rationale: Encrypting the DNS queries protects them from interception and tampering by untrusted third parties, for example on public Wi-Fi, so others can't see or redirect the names the PC looks up.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Secure DNS client over HTTPS (DoH)

checks.name: BitLocker OS Drive
checks.description: BitLocker Drive Encryption encrypts the Windows drive. With a TPM, the drive unlocks only when the PC boots normally with its own trusted boot components.
checks.rationale: Encryption helps protect against data theft or exposure if the device is lost or stolen, or decommissioned without wiping: without the key, the data on the drive can't be read, even if the drive is removed and read in another computer.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: BitLocker overview

checks.name: BitLocker Recovery Key Present
checks.description: A BitLocker recovery password (48-digit numerical password) restores access to a BitLocker-protected drive that can't be unlocked normally, for example after a firmware update, a hardware change or a TPM problem.
checks.rationale: Without a recovery password, the encrypted data can be lost for good when BitLocker asks for recovery. Store the recovery password in a safe place away from the PC.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: BitLocker recovery overview

cisBenchmark: CIS Microsoft Windows 11 Stand-alone Benchmark v5.0.0

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Enforce password history' is set to '24 or more password(s)'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines the number of renewed, unique passwords that have to be associated with a user account before you can reuse an old password. The value for this policy setting must be between 0 and 24 passwords. The default value for stand-alone systems is 0 passwords, but the default setting when joined to a domain is 24 passwords. To maintain the effectiveness of this policy setting, use the Minimum password age setting to prevent users from repeatedly changing their password.
The recommended state for this setting is: 24 or more password(s).
Note: Password Policy settings (section 1.1) and Account Lockout Policy settings (section 1.2) must be applied via the Default Domain Policy GPO in order to be globally in effect on domain user accounts as their default behavior. If these settings are configured in another GPO, they will only affect local user accounts on the computers that receive the GPO. However, custom exceptions to the default password policy and account lockout policy rules for specific domain users and/or groups can be defined using Password Settings Objects (PSOs), which are completely separate from Group Policy and most easily configured using Active Directory Administrative Center.
Note #2: As of the publication of this benchmark, Microsoft currently has a maximum limit of 24 saved passwords. For more information, please visit Enforce password history (Windows 10) - Windows security | Microsoft Docs.
cisRecommendations.rationale:
The longer a password is reused, the greater the chance that a threat actor can determine the password through brute force attacks. Also, accounts that may have been compromised will remain exploitable if the password is left unchanged. If password changes are required but password reuse is not prevented, or if a continually small number of passwords are reused, the effectiveness of a good password policy is greatly reduced.
If a low number for this policy setting is specified, users will be able to use the same small number of passwords repeatedly.
Note: If the Minimum password age setting is not configured, users might repeatedly change their passwords until they can reuse their original password.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Maximum password age' is set to '365 or fewer days, but not 0'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting defines how long a user can use their password before it expires.
Values for this policy setting range from 0 to 999 days. If you set the value to 0, the password will never expire.
The recommended state for this setting is 365 or fewer days, but not 0.
Note: Password Policy settings (section 1.1) and Account Lockout Policy settings (section 1.2) must be applied via the Default Domain Policy GPO in order to be globally in effect on domain user accounts as their default behavior. If these settings are configured in another GPO, they will only affect local user accounts on the computers that receive the GPO. However, custom exceptions to the default password policy and account lockout policy rules for specific domain users and/or groups can be defined using Password Settings Objects (PSOs), which are completely separate from Group Policy and most easily configured using Active Directory Administrative Center.
cisRecommendations.rationale:
The longer a password exists the higher the likelihood that it will be compromised by a brute force attack, a threat actor gaining general knowledge about the user, or by the user sharing the password. Configuring the Maximum password age setting to 0 so that users are never required to change their passwords is a major security risk because that allows a compromised password to be used by the threat actor for as long as the valid user has authorized access.
Because threat actors can crack passwords, the more frequently the password is changed, the less opportunity a threat actor has to use a cracked password. However, the lower this value is set, the higher the potential for an increase in calls to help desk support due to users having to change their password or forgetting which password is current.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Minimum password age' is set to '1 or more day(s)'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines the number of days that you must use a password before you can change it. The range of values for this policy setting is between 1 and 999 days. (You may also set the value to 0 to allow immediate password changes.) The default value for this setting is 0 days.
The recommended state for this setting is: 1 or more day(s)).
Note: Password Policy settings (section 1.1) and Account Lockout Policy settings (section 1.2) must be applied via the Default Domain Policy GPO in order to be globally in effect on domain user accounts as their default behavior. If these settings are configured in another GPO, they will only affect local user accounts on the computers that receive the GPO. However, custom exceptions to the default password policy and account lockout policy rules for specific domain users and/or groups can be defined using Password Settings Objects (PSOs), which are completely separate from Group Policy and most easily configured using Active Directory Administrative Center.
cisRecommendations.rationale:
Users may have favorite passwords that they like to use because they are easy to remember Unfortunately, passwords are compromised and if a threat actor is targeting a specific individual's user account, with foreknowledge of data about that user, reuse of old passwords can cause a security breach. To address password reuse, a combination of security settings is required.
Using this policy setting with the Enforce password history setting prevents the easy reuse of old passwords. For example, if you configure the Enforce password history setting to ensure that users cannot reuse any of their last 12 passwords, they could change their password 13 times in a few minutes and reuse the password they started with, unless you also configure the Minimum password age setting to a number that is greater than 0. You must configure this policy setting to a number that is greater than 0 for the Enforce password history setting to be effective.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Minimum password length' is set to '14 or more character(s)'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines the least number of characters that make up a password for a user account.
The recommended state for this setting is: 14 or more character(s).
Note: In Windows Server 2016 and older versions of Windows Server, the GUI of the Local Security Policy (LSP), Local Group Policy Editor (LGPE) and Group Policy Management Editor (GPME) would not let you set this value higher than 14 characters. However, starting with Windows Server 2019, Microsoft changed the GUI to allow up to a 20 character minimum password length.
Note #2: Password Policy settings (section 1.1) and Account Lockout Policy settings (section 1.2) must be applied via the Default Domain Policy GPO in order to be globally in effect on domain user accounts as their default behavior. If these settings are configured in another GPO, they will only affect local user accounts on the computers that receive the GPO. However, custom exceptions to the default password policy and account lockout policy rules for specific domain users and/or groups can be defined using Password Settings Objects (PSOs), which are completely separate from Group Policy and most easily configured using Active Directory Administrative Center.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Types of password attacks include dictionary attacks (which attempt to use common words and phrases) and brute force attacks (which try every possible combination of characters). Also, threat actors sometimes try to obtain the account database so they can use tools to discover the accounts and passwords.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Password must meet complexity requirements' is set to 'Enabled'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting checks all new passwords to ensure that they meet basic requirements for strong passwords.
When this policy is enabled, passwords must meet the following minimum requirements:
• Not contain the user's account name or parts of the user's full name that exceed two consecutive characters
• Be at least six characters in length
• Contain characters from three of the following categories:
o English uppercase characters (A through Z)
o English lowercase characters (a through z)
o Base 10 digits (0 through 9)
o Non-alphabetic characters (for example, !, $, #, %)
o A catch-all category of any Unicode character that does not fall under the previous four categories. This fifth category can be regionally specific.
Each additional character in a password increases its complexity exponentially. For instance, a seven-character, all lower-case alphabetic password would have 26 to the power of 7 (approximately 8 x 10 to the power of 9 or 8 billion) possible combinations. At 1,000,000 attempts per second (a capability of many password-cracking utilities), it would only take 133 minutes to crack. A seven-character alphabetic password with case sensitivity has 52 to the power of 7 combinations. A seven-character case-sensitive alphanumeric password without punctuation has 627 combinations. An eight-character password has 26 to the power of 8 (or 2 x 10 to the power of 11) possible combinations. Although this might seem to be a large number, at 1,000,000 attempts per second it would take only 59 hours to try all possible passwords. Remember, these times will significantly increase for passwords that use ALT characters and other special keyboard characters such as "!" or "@". Proper use of the password settings can help make it difficult to mount a brute force attack.
The recommended state for this setting is: Enabled.
Note: Password Policy settings (section 1.1) and Account Lockout Policy settings (section 1.2) must be applied via the Default Domain Policy GPO in order to be globally in effect on domain user accounts as their default behavior. If these settings are configured in another GPO, they will only affect local user accounts on the computers that receive the GPO. However, custom exceptions to the default password policy and account lockout policy rules for specific domain users and/or groups can be defined using Password Settings Objects (PSOs), which are completely separate from Group Policy and most easily configured using Active Directory Administrative Center.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Passwords that contain only alphanumeric characters are extremely easy to discover with several publicly available tools.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Relax minimum password length limits' is set to 'Enabled'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines whether the minimum password length setting can be increased beyond the legacy limit of 14 characters. For more information, please see the following Microsoft Security Blog.
The recommended state for this setting is: Enabled.
Note: This setting only affects local accounts on the computer. Domain accounts are only affected by settings on the Domain Controllers, because that is where domain accounts are stored.
cisRecommendations.rationale: This setting will enable the enforcement of longer and generally stronger passwords or passphrases where MFA is not in use.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Store passwords using reversible encryption' is set to 'Disabled'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines whether the operating system stores passwords in a way that uses reversible encryption, which provides support for application protocols that require knowledge of the user's password for authentication purposes. Passwords that are stored with reversible encryption are essentially the same as plaintext versions of the passwords.
The recommended state for this setting is: Disabled.
Note: Password Policy settings (section 1.1) and Account Lockout Policy settings (section 1.2) must be applied via the Default Domain Policy GPO in order to be globally in effect on domain user accounts as their default behavior. If these settings are configured in another GPO, they will only affect local user accounts on the computers that receive the GPO. However, custom exceptions to the default password policy and account lockout policy rules for specific domain users and/or groups can be defined using Password Settings Objects (PSOs), which are completely separate from Group Policy and most easily configured using Active Directory Administrative Center.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Enabling this policy setting allows the operating system to store passwords in a weaker format that is much more susceptible to compromise and weakens your system security.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Account lockout duration' is set to '15 or more minute(s)'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines the length of time that must pass before a locked account is unlocked and a user can try to log on again. The setting does this by specifying the number of minutes a locked-out account will remain unavailable. If the value for this policy setting is configured to 0, locked out accounts will remain locked out until an administrator manually unlocks them.
Although it might seem like a good idea to configure the value for this policy setting to a high value, such a configuration will likely increase the number of calls that the help desk receives to unlock accounts locked by mistake. Users should be aware of the length of time a lock remains in place, so that they realize they only need to call the help desk if they have an extremely urgent need to regain access to their computer.
The recommended state for this setting is: 15 or more minute(s).
Note: Password Policy settings (section 1.1) and Account Lockout Policy settings (section 1.2) must be applied via the Default Domain Policy GPO in order to be globally in effect on domain user accounts as their default behavior. If these settings are configured in another GPO, they will only affect local user accounts on the computers that receive the GPO. However, custom exceptions to the default password policy and account lockout policy rules for specific domain users and/or groups can be defined using Password Settings Objects (PSOs), which are completely separate from Group Policy and most easily configured using Active Directory Administrative Center.
cisRecommendations.rationale: A denial-of-service (DoS) condition can be created if a threat actor abuses the Account lockout threshold and repeatedly attempts to log on with a specific account. Once the Account lockout threshold setting is configured, the account will be locked out after the specified number of failed attempts. If Account lockout duration is set to 0, then the account will remain locked out until an administrator unlocks it manually.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Account lockout threshold' is set to '5 or fewer invalid logon attempt(s), but not 0'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines the number of failed logon attempts before the account is locked.
The recommended state for this setting is: 5 or fewer invalid logon attempt(s), but not 0.
Note: A value of 0 does not conform to the benchmark as it disables account lockout threshold.
Note #2: Password Policy settings (section 1.1) and Account Lockout Policy settings (section 1.2) must be applied via the Default Domain Policy GPO in order to be globally in effect on domain user accounts as their default behavior. If these settings are configured in another GPO, they will only affect local user accounts on the computers that receive the GPO. However, custom exceptions to the default password policy and account lockout policy rules for specific domain users and/or groups can be defined using Password Settings Objects (PSOs), which are completely separate from Group Policy and most easily configured using Active Directory Administrative Center.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Setting an account lockout threshold reduces the likelihood that an online password brute force attack will be successful. Setting the account lockout threshold too low introduces risk of increased accidental lockouts and/or a threat actor intentionally locking out accounts.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Allow Administrator account lockout' is set to 'Enabled'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines whether the built-in Administrator account is subject to the following Account Lockout Policy settings: Account lockout duration, Account lockout threshold, and Reset account lockout counter. By default, this account is excluded from the account lockout controls and will never be locked out with repeated bad password attempts.
The recommended state for this setting is: Enabled.
Note: This setting applies only to OSes patched as of October 11, 2022 (see MS KB5020282).
cisRecommendations.rationale: Enabling account lockout policies for the built-in Administrator account will reduce the likelihood of a successful brute force attack.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Reset account lockout counter after' is set to '15 or more minute(s)'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines the length of time before the Account lockout threshold resets to zero. If the Account lockout threshold is defined, this reset time must be less than or equal to the value for the Account lockout duration setting.
The recommended state for this setting is: 15 or more minute(s).
Note: Password Policy settings (section 1.1) and Account Lockout Policy settings (section 1.2) must be applied via the Default Domain Policy GPO in order to be globally in effect on domain user accounts as their default behavior. If these settings are configured in another GPO, they will only affect local user accounts on the computers that receive the GPO. However, custom exceptions to the default password policy and account lockout policy rules for specific domain users and/or groups can be defined using Password Settings Objects (PSOs), which are completely separate from Group Policy and most easily configured using Active Directory Administrative Center.
cisRecommendations.rationale:
If the account lockout policy is left at its default setting or configured with an excessively long interval, the environment may be vulnerable to denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. A threat actor could repeatedly attempt to login across multiple accounts, triggering lockouts and disrupting access.
Without a defined lockout threshold, administrators would need to manually reset affected accounts. However, by setting a reasonable lockout duration, accounts will automatically unlock after a specified period, reducing administrative overhead and maintaining security.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Access Credential Manager as a trusted caller' is set to 'No One'
cisRecommendations.description: This security setting is used by Credential Manager during Backup and Restore. No accounts should have this user right, as it is only assigned to Winlogon. Users' saved credentials might be compromised if this user right is assigned to other entities. The recommended state for this setting is: No One.
cisRecommendations.rationale: If an account is given this right the user of the account may create an application that calls into Credential Manager and is returned the credentials for another user.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Access this computer from the network' is set to 'Administrators, Remote Desktop Users'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting allows other users on the network to connect to the computer and is required by various network protocols that include Server Message Block (SMB)-based protocols, NetBIOS, Common Internet File System (CIFS), and Component Object Model Plus (COM+).
The recommended state for this setting is: Administrators, Remote Desktop Users.
Note: If your organization is using Microsoft Defender for Identity (formerly Azure Advanced Threat Protection (Azure ATP)), the (organization-named) Defender for Identity Directory Service Account (DSA), will also need to be granted the same Access this computer from the network User Right Assignment. For more information on adding the service account please see Make sure the DSA is allowed to access computers from the network in Microsoft Defender for Identity | Microsoft Docs.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Users who can connect from their computer to the network can access resources on target computers for which they have permission. For example, the Access this computer from the network user right is required for users to connect to shared printers and folders. If this user right is assigned to the Everyone group, then anyone will be able to read the files in those shared folders. However, this situation is unlikely for new installations of Windows Server 2003 with Service Pack 1 (SP1), because the default share and NTFS permissions in Windows Server 2003 do not include the Everyone group. This vulnerability may have a higher level of risk for computers that you upgrade from Windows NT 4.0 or Windows 2000, because the default permissions for these operating systems are not as restrictive as the default permissions in Windows Server 2003.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Act as part of the operating system' is set to 'No One'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting allows a process to assume the identity of any user and thus gain access to the resources that the user is authorized to access.
The recommended state for this setting is: No One.
Note: This user right is considered a "sensitive privilege" for the purposes of auditing.
cisRecommendations.rationale: The Act as part of the operating system user right is extremely powerful. Anyone with this user right can take complete control of the computer and erase evidence of their activities.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Adjust memory quotas for a process' is set to 'Administrators, LOCAL SERVICE, NETWORK SERVICE'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting allows a user to adjust the maximum amount of memory that is available to a process. The ability to adjust memory quotas is useful for system tuning, but it can be abused. In the wrong hands, it could be used to launch a denial-of-service (DoS) attack.
The recommended state for this setting is: Administrators, LOCAL SERVICE, NETWORK SERVICE.
cisRecommendations.rationale: A user with the Adjust memory quotas for a process user right can reduce the amount of memory that is available to any process, which could cause business-critical network applications to become slow or to fail. In the wrong hands, this privilege could be used to start a DoS attack.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Allow log on locally' is set to 'Administrators, Users'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines which users can interactively log on to computers in your environment. Logons that are initiated by pressing the CTRL+ALT+DEL key sequence on the client computer keyboard require this user right. Users who attempt to log on through Terminal Services / Remote Desktop Services or IIS also require this user right. The recommended state for this setting is: Administrators, Users.
Note: The Guest account is also assigned this user right by default. Although this account is disabled by default, it's recommended that you configure this setting through Group Policy. However, this user right should generally be restricted to the Administrators and Users groups. Assign this user right to the Backup Operators group if your organization requires that they have this capability.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Any account with the Allow log on locally user right can log on at the console of the computer. If you do not restrict this user right to legitimate users who need to be able to log on to the console of the computer, unauthorized users could download and run malicious software to elevate their privileges.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Allow log on through Remote Desktop Services' is set to 'Administrators, Remote Desktop Users'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines which users or groups have the right to log on as a Remote Desktop Services client. If your organization uses Remote Assistance as part of its help desk strategy, create a group and assign it this user right through Group Policy. If the help desk in your organization does not use Remote Assistance, assign this user right only to the Administrators group or use the Restricted Groups feature to ensure that no user accounts are part of the Remote Desktop Users group.
Restrict this user right to the Administrators group, and possibly the Remote Desktop Users group, to prevent unwanted users from gaining access to computers on your network by means of the Remote Assistance feature.
The recommended state for this setting is: Administrators, Remote Desktop Users.
Note: The above list is to be treated as a whitelist, which implies that the above principals need not be present for assessment of this recommendation to pass.
Note #2: In all versions of Windows prior to Windows 7, Remote Desktop Services was known as Terminal Services, so you should substitute the older term if comparing against an older OS.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Any account with the Allow log on through Remote Desktop Services user right can log on to the remote console of the computer. If you do not restrict this user right to legitimate users who need to log on to the console of the computer, unauthorized users could download and run malicious software to elevate their privileges.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Back up files and directories' is set to 'Administrators'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting allows users to circumvent file and directory permissions to back up the system. This user right is enabled only when an application (such as NTBACKUP) attempts to access a file or directory through the NTFS file system backup application programming interface (API). Otherwise, the assigned file and directory permissions apply.
The recommended state for this setting is: Administrators.
Note: This user right is considered a "sensitive privilege" for the purposes of auditing.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Users who are able to back up data from a computer could take the backup media to a non-domain computer on which they have administrative privileges and restore the data. They could take ownership of the files and view any unencrypted data that is contained within the backup set.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Change the system time' is set to 'Administrators, LOCAL SERVICE'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines which users and groups can change the time and date on the internal clock of the computers in your environment. Users who are assigned this user right can affect the appearance of event logs. When a computer's time setting is changed, logged events reflect the new time, not the actual time that the events occurred.
The recommended state for this setting is: Administrators, LOCAL SERVICE.
Note: Discrepancies between the time on the local computer and on the Domain Controllers in your environment may cause problems for the Kerberos authentication protocol, which could make it impossible for users to log on to the domain or obtain authorization to access domain resources after they are logged on. Also, problems will occur when Group Policy is applied to client computers if the system time is not synchronized with the Domain Controllers.
cisRecommendations.rationale:
Users who can change the time on a computer could cause several problems. For example, time stamps on event log entries could be made inaccurate, time stamps on files and folders that are created or modified could be incorrect, and computers that belong to a domain may not be able to authenticate themselves or users who try to log on to the domain from them. Also, because the Kerberos authentication protocol requires that the requestor and authenticator have their clocks synchronized within an administrator-defined skew period, a threat actor who changes a computer's time may cause that computer to be unable to obtain or grant Kerberos tickets.
The risk from these types of events is mitigated on most Domain Controllers, Member Servers, and end-user computers because the Windows Time service automatically synchronizes time with Domain Controllers in the following ways:
• All client desktop computers and Member Servers use the authenticating Domain Controller as their inbound time partner.
• All Domain Controllers in a domain nominate the Primary Domain Controller (PDC) Emulator operations master as their inbound time partner.
• All PDC Emulator operations masters follow the hierarchy of domains in the selection of their inbound time partner.
• The PDC Emulator operations master at the root of the domain is authoritative for the organization. Therefore it is recommended that you configure this computer to synchronize with a reliable external time server.
This vulnerability becomes much more serious if a threat actor is able to change the system time and then stop the Windows Time service or reconfigure it to synchronize with a time server that is not accurate.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Create a pagefile' is set to 'Administrators'
cisRecommendations.description: This policy setting allows users to change the size of the pagefile. The page file is a hidden system file on the hard drive that serves as an extension of the system’s RAM. When physical memory is full, the system moves less frequently used data to the page file to free up RAM for active processes The recommended state for this setting is: Administrators.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Users who can change the page file size could make it extremely small or move the file to a highly fragmented storage volume, which could cause reduced computer performance.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Create a token object' is set to 'No One'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting allows a process to create an access token, which may provide elevated rights to access sensitive data.
The recommended state for this setting is: No One.
Note: This user right is considered a "sensitive privilege" for the purposes of auditing.
cisRecommendations.rationale:
A user account that is given this user right has complete control over the system and can lead to the system being compromised. It is highly recommended that you do not assign any user accounts this right.
The operating system examines a user's access token to determine the level of the user's privileges. Access tokens are built when users log on to the local computer or connect to a remote computer over a network. When you revoke a privilege, the change is immediately recorded, but the change is not reflected in the user's access token until the next time the user logs on or connects. Users with the ability to create or modify tokens can change the level of access for any currently logged on account. They could escalate their own privileges or create a DoS condition.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Create global objects' is set to 'Administrators, LOCAL SERVICE, NETWORK SERVICE, SERVICE'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines whether users can create global objects that are available to all sessions. Users can still create objects that are specific to their own session if they do not have this user right.
Users who can create global objects could affect processes that run under other users' sessions. This capability could lead to a variety of problems, such as application failure or data corruption.
The recommended state for this setting is: Administrators, LOCAL SERVICE, NETWORK SERVICE, SERVICE.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Users who can create global objects could affect Windows services and processes that run under other user or system accounts. This capability could lead to a variety of problems, such as application failure, data corruption and elevation of privilege.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Create permanent shared objects' is set to 'No One'
cisRecommendations.description:
This user right is useful to kernel-mode components that extend the object namespace. However, components that run in kernel mode have this user right inherently. Therefore, it is typically not necessary to specifically assign this user right.
The recommended state for this setting is: No One.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Users who have the Create permanent shared objects user right could create new shared objects and expose sensitive data to the network.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Create symbolic links' is set to 'Administrators'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines which users can create symbolic links. In Windows Vista, existing NTFS file system objects, such as files and folders, can be accessed by referring to a new kind of file system object called a symbolic link. A symbolic link is a pointer (much like a shortcut or .lnk file) to another file system object, which can be a file, folder, shortcut or another symbolic link. The difference between a shortcut and a symbolic link is that a shortcut only works from within the Windows shell. To other programs and applications, shortcuts are just another file, whereas with symbolic links, the concept of a shortcut is implemented as a feature of the NTFS file system.
Symbolic links can potentially expose security vulnerabilities in applications that are not designed to use them. For this reason, the privilege for creating symbolic links should only be assigned to trusted users. By default, only Administrators can create symbolic links.
The recommended state for this setting is: Administrators and (when the Hyper-V feature is installed) NT VIRTUAL MACHINE\Virtual Machines.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Users who have the Create symbolic links user right could inadvertently or maliciously expose your system to symbolic link attacks. Symbolic link attacks can be used to change the permissions on a file, to corrupt data, to destroy data, or as a denial-of-service (DoS) attack.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Debug programs' is set to 'Administrators'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines which user accounts will have the right to attach a debugger to any process or to the kernel, which provides complete access to sensitive and critical operating system components. Developers who are debugging their own applications do not need to be assigned this user right; however, developers who are debugging new system components will need it.
The recommended state for this setting is: Administrators.
Note: This user right is considered a "sensitive privilege" for the purposes of auditing.
cisRecommendations.rationale: The Debug programs user right can be exploited to capture sensitive computer information from system memory, or to access and modify kernel or application structures. Some attack tools exploit this user right to extract hashed passwords and other private security information, or to insert rootkit code. By default, the Debug programs user right is assigned only to administrators, which helps to mitigate the risk from this vulnerability.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Deny access to this computer from the network' to include 'Guests'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting prohibits users from connecting to a computer from across the network, which would allow users to access and potentially modify data remotely. In high security environments, there should be no need for remote users to access data on a computer. Instead, file sharing should be accomplished through the use of network servers. This user right supersedes the Access this computer from the network user right if an account is subject to both policies.
The recommended state for this setting is to include: Guests.
Note: The security identifier Local account is not available in Windows 7 and Windows 8.0 unless MSKB 2871997 has been installed.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Users who can log on to the computer over the network can enumerate lists of account names, group names, and shared resources. Users with permission to access shared folders and files can connect over the network and possibly view or modify data.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Deny log on as a batch job' to include 'Guests'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines which accounts will not be able to log on to the computer as a batch job. A batch job is not a batch (.bat) file, but rather a batch-queue facility. Accounts that use the Task Scheduler to schedule jobs need this user right.
This user right supersedes the Log on as a batch job user right, which could be used to allow accounts to schedule jobs that consume excessive system resources. Such an occurrence could cause a DoS condition. Failure to assign this user right to the recommended accounts can be a security risk.
The recommended state for this setting is to include: Guests.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Accounts that have the Log on as a batch job user right could be used to schedule jobs that could consume excessive computer resources and cause a DoS condition.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Deny log on as a service' to include 'Guests'
cisRecommendations.description:
This security setting determines which service accounts are prevented from registering a process as a service. This user right supersedes the Log on as a service user right if an account is subject to both policies.
The recommended state for this setting is to include: Guests.
Note: This security setting does not apply to the System, Local Service, or Network Service accounts.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Accounts that can log on as a service could be used to configure and start new unauthorized services, such as a keylogger or other malicious software. The benefit of the specified countermeasure is somewhat reduced by the fact that only users with administrative privileges can install and configure services, and a threat actor who has already attained that level of access could configure the service to run with the System account.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Deny log on locally' to include 'Guests'
cisRecommendations.description:
This security setting determines which users are prevented from logging on at the computer. This policy setting supersedes the Allow log on locally policy setting if an account is subject to both policies.
The recommended state for this setting is to include: Guests.
Important: If you apply this security policy to the Everyone group, no one will be able to log on locally.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Any account with the ability to log on locally could be used to log on at the console of the computer. If this user right is not restricted to legitimate users who need to log on to the console of the computer, unauthorized users might download and run malicious software that elevates their privileges.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services' to include 'Guests'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines whether users can log on as Remote Desktop clients. After the baseline workstation is joined to a domain environment, there is no need to use local accounts to access the workstation from the network. Domain accounts can access the workstation for administration and end-user processing. This user right supersedes the Allow log on through Remote Desktop Services user right if an account is subject to both policies.
The recommended state for this setting is to include: Guests.
Note: The security identifier Local account is not available in Windows 7 and Windows 8.0 unless MSKB 2871997 has been installed.
Note #2: In all versions of Windows prior to Windows 7, Remote Desktop Services was known as Terminal Services, so you should substitute the older term if comparing against an older OS.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Any account with the right to log on through Remote Desktop Services could be used to log on to the remote console of the computer. If this user right is not restricted to legitimate users who need to log on to the console of the computer, unauthorized users might download and run malicious software that elevates their privileges.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Enable computer and user accounts to be trusted for delegation' is set to 'No One'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting allows users to change the Trusted for Delegation setting on a computer object in Active Directory.
The recommended state for this setting is: No One.
Note: This user right is considered a "sensitive privilege" for the purposes of auditing.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Misuse of this user right could allow unauthorized users to impersonate other users on the network. A threat actor could exploit this privilege to gain access to network resources and make it difficult to determine what has happened after a security incident.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Force shutdown from a remote system' is set to 'Administrators'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting allows users to shut down Windows Vista-based or newer computers from remote locations on the network. Anyone who has been assigned this user right can cause a denial-of-service (DoS) condition, which would make the computer unavailable to service user requests. Therefore, it is recommended that only highly trusted administrators be assigned this user right.
The recommended state for this setting is: Administrators.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Any user who can shut down a computer could cause a DoS condition to occur. Therefore, this user right should be tightly restricted.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Impersonate a client after authentication' is set to 'Administrators, LOCAL SERVICE, NETWORK SERVICE, SERVICE, RESTRICTED SERVICES\PrintSpoolerService'
cisRecommendations.description:
The policy setting allows programs that run on behalf of a user to impersonate that user (or another specified account) so that they can act on behalf of the user. If this user right is required for this kind of impersonation, an unauthorized user will not be able to convince a client to connect—for example, by remote procedure call (RPC) or named pipes—to a service that they have created to impersonate that client, which could elevate the unauthorized user's permissions to administrative or system levels.
Services that are started by the Service Control Manager have the built-in Service group added by default to their access tokens. COM servers that are started by the COM infrastructure and configured to run under a specific account also have the Service group added to their access tokens. As a result, these processes are assigned this user right when they are started.
Also, a user can impersonate an access token if any of the following conditions exist:
• The access token that is being impersonated is for this user.
• The user, in this logon session, logged on to the network with explicit credentials to create the access token.
• The requested level is less than Impersonate, such as Anonymous or Identify.
The recommended state for this setting is: Administrators, LOCAL SERVICE, NETWORK SERVICE, SERVICE, and RESTRICTED SERVICES\PrintSpoolerService.
Note: This user right is considered a "sensitive privilege" for the purposes of auditing.
cisRecommendations.rationale: A threat actor with the Impersonate a client after authentication user right could create a service, trick a client to make them connect to the service, and then impersonate that client to elevate the threat actor's level of access to that of the client.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Increase scheduling priority' is set to 'Administrators, Window Manager\Window Manager Group'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines whether users can increase the base priority class of a process. (It is not a privileged operation to increase relative priority within a priority class.) This user right is not required by administrative tools that are supplied with the operating system but might be required by software development tools.
The recommended state for this setting is: Administrators, Window Manager\Window Manager Group.
cisRecommendations.rationale: A user who is assigned this user right could increase the scheduling priority of a process to Real-Time, which would leave little processing time for all other processes and could lead to a DoS condition.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Load and unload device drivers' is set to 'Administrators'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting allows users to dynamically load a new device driver on a system. This user right is not required if a signed driver for the new hardware already exists in the Driver.cab file on the system.
The recommended state for this setting is: Administrators.
Note: This user right is considered a "sensitive privilege" for the purposes of auditing.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Device drivers run as highly privileged code. A user or threat actor who has the Load and unload device drivers user right could unintentionally install malicious code that masquerades as a device driver. Administrators should exercise greater care and install only drivers with verified digital signatures.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Lock pages in memory' is set to 'No One'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting allows a process to keep data in physical memory, which prevents the system from paging the data to virtual memory on disk. If this user right is assigned, significant degradation of system performance can occur.
The recommended state for this setting is: No One.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Users with the Lock pages in memory user right could assign physical memory to several processes, which could leave little or no RAM for other processes and result in a DoS condition.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Modify an object label' is set to 'No One'
cisRecommendations.description:
This privilege determines which user accounts can modify the integrity label of objects, such as files, registry keys, or processes owned by other users. Processes running under a user account can modify the label of an object owned by that user to a lower level without this privilege.
The recommended state for this setting is: No One.
cisRecommendations.rationale: By modifying the integrity label of an object owned by another user a threat actor may cause them to execute code at a higher level of privilege than intended.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Modify firmware environment values' is set to 'Administrators'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting allows users to configure the system-wide environment variables that affect hardware configuration. This information is typically stored in the Last Known Good Configuration. Modification of these values and could lead to a hardware failure that would result in a denial-of-service condition.
The recommended state for this setting is: Administrators.
Note: This user right is considered a "sensitive privilege" for the purposes of auditing.
cisRecommendations.rationale: Anyone who is assigned the Modify firmware environment values user right could configure the settings of a hardware component to cause it to fail, which could lead to data corruption or a DoS condition.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Perform volume maintenance tasks' is set to 'Administrators'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting allows users to manage the system's volume or disk configuration, which could allow a user to delete a volume and cause data loss as well as a denial-of-service condition.
The recommended state for this setting is: Administrators.
Note: A workstation with Microsoft SQL Server installed will require a special exception to this recommendation for the account that runs the SQL Server service to be granted this user right.
cisRecommendations.rationale: A user who is assigned the Perform volume maintenance tasks user right could delete a volume, which could result in the loss of data or a DoS condition.

cisRecommendations.title: Ensure 'Profile single process' is set to 'Administrators'
cisRecommendations.description:
This policy setting determines which users can use tools to monitor the performance of non-system processes. Typically, this setting does not need to be configured to use the Microsoft Management Console (MMC) Performance snap-in. However, this user right is needed if System Monitor is configured to collect data using Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI).
The recommended state for this setting is: Administrators.
cisRecommendations.rationale: The Profile single process user right presents a moderate vulnerability. A threat actor with this user right could monitor a computer's performance to help identify critical processes that they might wish to attack directly. The threat actor may also be able to determine what processes run on the computer so that they can identify countermeasures that they may need to avoid, such as antivirus software, an intrusion-detection system, or which other users are logged on to a computer.
